claim: RYR1-related myopathies (RYR1-RMs) are a common group of childhood muscle diseases associated with severe disabilities and early mortality.
source: Ryanodine receptor type I-related myopathies (RYR1-RMs) are a common group of childhood muscle diseases associated with severe disabilities and early mortality for which there are no available treatments.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a characterization of RYR1-RMs.

claim: There are no available treatments for RYR1-related myopathies.
source: Ryanodine receptor type I-related myopathies (RYR1-RMs) are a common group of childhood muscle diseases associated with severe disabilities and early mortality for which there are no available treatments.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract.

claim: A multi-species discovery pipeline using nematode, zebrafish, and mammalian cell models was developed for identifying therapeutic targets for RYR1-RMs.
source: To accomplish this, we developed a discovery pipeline using nematode, zebrafish, and mammalian cell models.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a methodological approach.

claim: Large-scale drug screens in C. elegans uncovered 74 hits.
source: We first performed large-scale drug screens in C. elegans which uncovered 74 hits.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the screening results in the abstract.

claim: Targeted testing in zebrafish yielded positive results for two p38 inhibitors.
source: Targeted testing in zebrafish yielded positive results for two p38 inhibitors.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a result of zebrafish testing.

claim: Pharmacological inhibition of p38 impaired caffeine-induced Ca2+ release from wild type mouse myotubes.
source: Using mouse myotubes, we found that either pharmacological inhibition or siRNA silencing of p38 impaired caffeine-induced Ca2+ release from wild type cells while promoting intracellular Ca2+ release in Ryr1 knockout cells.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figure 5.

claim: siRNA silencing of p38 impaired caffeine-induced Ca2+ release from wild type mouse myotubes.
source: Using mouse myotubes, we found that either pharmacological inhibition or siRNA silencing of p38 impaired caffeine-induced Ca2+ release from wild type cells while promoting intracellular Ca2+ release in Ryr1 knockout cells.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figure 5.

claim: Pharmacological inhibition of p38 promoted intracellular Ca2+ release in Ryr1 knockout mouse myotubes.
source: Using mouse myotubes, we found that either pharmacological inhibition or siRNA silencing of p38 impaired caffeine-induced Ca2+ release from wild type cells while promoting intracellular Ca2+ release in Ryr1 knockout cells.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figure 5.

claim: siRNA silencing of p38 promoted intracellular Ca2+ release in Ryr1 knockout mouse myotubes.
source: Using mouse myotubes, we found that either pharmacological inhibition or siRNA silencing of p38 impaired caffeine-induced Ca2+ release from wild type cells while promoting intracellular Ca2+ release in Ryr1 knockout cells.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figure 5.

claim: p38 inhibition blunts the aberrant temperature-dependent increase in resting Ca2+ in myotubes from an RYR1-RM mouse model.
source: Lastly, we demonstrated that p38 inhibition blunts the aberrant temperature-dependent increase in resting Ca2+ in myotubes from an RYR1-RM mouse model.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figure 5D.

claim: The ryanodine receptor type I (RyR1) is a calcium release channel located in the terminal cisternae of the sarcoplasmic reticulum in skeletal muscle.
source: The ryanodine receptor type I (RyR1) is a calcium release channel located in the terminal cisternae of the sarcoplasmic reticulum (SR) in skeletal muscle.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge.

claim: During excitation-contraction coupling, RyR1 is activated by the voltage sensing L-type calcium channel dihydropyridine receptor (DHPR).
source: During excitation-contraction coupling (ECC), RyR1 is activated by the voltage sensing L-type calcium channel dihydropyridine receptor (DHPR), located in the transverse tubule (T-tubule) membrane.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge about ECC mechanism.

claim: Mutations in the RYR1 gene are the most common cause of non-dystrophic muscle disease in humans.
source: Mutations in the RYR1 gene are the most common cause of non-dystrophic muscle disease in humans (Colombo et al., 2015; Gonorazky et al., 2018; Jungbluth et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: There are currently no approved pharmacological therapies for patients with RYR1-RM.
source: Despite their relatively high prevalence and associated morbidities, there are currently no approved pharmacological therapies for patients with RYR1-RM.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a clinical gap.

claim: The C. elegans unc-68 mutant is a recessive model of RYR1-RM with impaired motility.
source: Well described recessive models of RYR1-RM include the C. elegans unc-68 mutant (null mutant with impaired motility [Maryon et al., 1996; Maryon et al., 1998])
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: The relatively relaxed zebrafish is a loss of function ryr1b mutant with impaired motility and early death.
source: the relatively relaxed zebrafish (loss of function ryr1b mutant with impaired motility and early death (Hirata et al., 2007)
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citation.

claim: The 'dyspedic' Ryr1 null mouse is perinatal lethal.
source: the 'dyspedic' Ryr1 null mouse (perinatal lethal [Buck et al., 1997; Avila and Dirksen, 2000])
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: Two compound heterozygous mouse models of recessive RYR1-RM were recently generated and characterized.
source: In addition, two compound heterozygous mouse models of recessive RYR1-RM were with recently generated and characterized (Brennan et al., 2019; Elbaz et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: N-acetylcysteine was tested in a clinical trial for RYR1-RM and failed to achieve its primary endpoint.
source: N-acetylcysteine was tested in a recently completed clinical trial (ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT02362425), where it failed to achieve its primary endpoint (Todd et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citation.

claim: The unc-68(r1162) C. elegans model has a deletion in the worm ryanodine receptor.
source: This model has a deletion in the worm ryanodine receptor, lacks RyR protein expression by western blot, and manifests an unc-68 null phenotype characterized by an 'uncoordinated' (unc) movement phenotype, defective pharyngeal pumping, impaired calcium regulation, and reduced fitness (Maryon et al., 1996; Maryon et al., 1998).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citations.

claim: The unc-68(r1162) C. elegans model lacks RyR protein expression by western blot.
source: This model has a deletion in the worm ryanodine receptor, lacks RyR protein expression by western blot, and manifests an unc-68 null phenotype characterized by an 'uncoordinated' (unc) movement phenotype, defective pharyngeal pumping, impaired calcium regulation, and reduced fitness (Maryon et al., 1996; Maryon et al., 1998).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citations.

claim: Nemadipine-A is an inhibitor of the dihydropyridine receptor.
source: we developed a sensitized screen based on our observation that nemadipine-A, an inhibitor of the dihydropyridine receptor (Kwok et al., 2006), induces developmental growth arrest in unc-68 mutants
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citation.

claim: unc-68 worms exposed to 25 μM nemadipine-A arrest at the L1-L3 larval stage.
source: Specifically, unc-68 worms exposed to 25 μM nemadipine-A arrest at the L1-L3 larval stage, while the majority of wild type N2 strain treated with nemadipine-A have either normal development or, in a small percentage, arrest at the L4 stage (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: 3700 chemicals were evaluated in duplicate from a combination of libraries in the C. elegans screen.
source: We evaluated 3700 chemicals in duplicate from a combination of libraries.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a description of the screening methodology.

claim: The primary screen found 278 chemical conditions out of 3700 (~7.5%) that contained at least one L4 or adult worm in duplicate wells.
source: The primary screen found 278 chemical conditions out of 3700 (~7.5%) that contained at least one L4 or adult worm in duplicate wells (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 2B.

claim: 74 chemicals reproducibly suppressed the nemadipine-A-induced growth suppression of unc-68 mutants upon re-testing.
source: We re-tested the 145 chemicals in duplicate and found that 74 reproducibly suppressed the nemadipine-A-induced growth suppression of unc-68 mutants (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 2B.

claim: Among the 74 'hits', there were 5 wactives, 7 non-wactives, 44 kinase inhibitors, and 18 compounds from the MicroSource library.
source: Among these 74 'hits', we identified five wactives and seven non-wactives, 44 kinase inhibitors, and 18 compounds from the MicroSource library (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a breakdown of the hits.

claim: p38 inhibitors were significantly overrepresented among the hits from the kinase inhibitor library.
source: Using this methodology, we found that p38 inhibitors were significantly overrepresented (**p=0.0022, Fisher's exact test) when considering the total number of p38 inhibitors in the kinase inhibitor library.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by statistical analysis.

claim: Structurally dissimilar p38 inhibitors suppressed the unc-68 phenotype.
source: Interestingly, structurally dissimilar p38 inhibitors suppressed the phenotype (clusters 5, 6, 16, and 19 in Figure 2C), suggesting that inhibition of their common target was responsible for the activity.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 2C showing structural clustering.

claim: RNAi knockdown of p38 MAPK orthologs pmk-1, pmk-2, pmk-3 alone and in combination increased the proportion of unc-68 mutants that escaped nemadipine-A induced growth arrest.
source: Finally, we validated p38 as a target by knocking down the p38 MAPK orthologs pmk-1, pmk-2, pmk-3 alone and in combination, and we observed a modest increase in the proportion of unc-68 mutants that escaped nemadipine-A induced growth arrest with each of the four conditions (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 2D.

claim: A screen of 436 kinase inhibitors at 10 μM from the DiscoveryProbe Kinase Inhibitor Library in ryr1a; ryr1b double mutant zebrafish did not identify any compounds that promoted movement.
source: We screened 436 kinase inhibitors at 10 μM from the DiscoveryProbe Kinase Inhibitor Library (ApexBio) and 1360 drugs at 10 μM from the US Drug Collection (MicroSource Discovery Systems), using improvement in motility of the ryr1a; ryr1b double mutants (as measured by touch-evoked escape response) as the primary outcome measure. We did not identify a single compound that was able to promote movement in these fish.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a negative result from the zebrafish screen.

claim: A screen of 1360 drugs at 10 μM from the US Drug Collection in ryr1a; ryr1b double mutant zebrafish did not identify any compounds that promoted movement.
source: We screened 436 kinase inhibitors at 10 μM from the DiscoveryProbe Kinase Inhibitor Library (ApexBio) and 1360 drugs at 10 μM from the US Drug Collection (MicroSource Discovery Systems), using improvement in motility of the ryr1a; ryr1b double mutants (as measured by touch-evoked escape response) as the primary outcome measure. We did not identify a single compound that was able to promote movement in these fish.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a negative result from the zebrafish screen.

claim: None of the tested chemicals improved the ryr1a; ryr1b double mutant phenotype at 10 μM.
source: First, we tested all of these at a single concentration of 10 μM for the ability to promote movement in the ryr1a; ryr1b double mutants, which in the untreated state lack any movement. Consistent with our large-scale screen done with the ryr1a; ryr1b mutants, none of these chemicals improved the double mutant phenotype (Figure 3).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 3.

claim: The p38 inhibitors SB239063 and PH-797804 decreased motility in wildtype zebrafish controls but had no effect on ryr1b mutants.
source: The p38 inhibitors SB239063 and PH-797804 decreased motility in wildtype controls, but had no effect on ryr1 mutants (Figure 4A–B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 4A-B.

claim: The absence of effects of SB239063 and PH-797804 in ryr1 mutant zebrafish stands in contrast to predicted additive and multiplicative effects.
source: The absence of effects in ryr1 mutant models stands in contrast to predicted additive and multiplicative effects for these compounds (Figure 4A'–B'), suggesting that RyR1-related pathways mediate the effects of SB239063 and PH-797804.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 4A'-B'.

claim: A new Ryr1 knockout C2C12 cell line was created using CRISPR/Cas9 gene editing.
source: We examined this in wild type C2C12 cells and in a C2C12 Ryr1 knockout line that we created using CRISPR/Cas9 gene editing.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a methodological development.

claim: The Ryr1 knockout C2C12 line contains a bi-allelic frameshift deletion mutation in Ryr1.
source: This new line contains a bi-allelic frameshift deletion mutation in Ryr1 (which we refer to as 'KO').
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a characterization of the knockout line.

claim: Successful targeting of the Ryr1 locus was demonstrated by Sanger sequencing.
source: Successful targeting of the Ryr1 locus was demonstrated by Sanger sequencing, lack of off-target mutations verified by whole genome sequencing, and absence of RyR1 protein expression confirmed by western blot analysis (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Lack of off-target mutations in the Ryr1 knockout C2C12 line was verified by whole genome sequencing.
source: Successful targeting of the Ryr1 locus was demonstrated by Sanger sequencing, lack of off-target mutations verified by whole genome sequencing, and absence of RyR1 protein expression confirmed by western blot analysis (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Absence of RyR1 protein expression in the Ryr1 knockout C2C12 line was confirmed by western blot analysis.
source: Successful targeting of the Ryr1 locus was demonstrated by Sanger sequencing, lack of off-target mutations verified by whole genome sequencing, and absence of RyR1 protein expression confirmed by western blot analysis (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Ryr1 KO myotubes treated with DMSO vehicle control lacked caffeine-induced Ca2+ release.
source: As expected, Ryr1 KO myotubes treated with DMSO vehicle control lacked caffeine-induced Ca2+ release (Figure 5A–B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 5A-B.

claim: Ryr1 KO myotubes treated with SB203580 or SB202190 exhibited a dose dependent increase in caffeine-induced calcium release.
source: KO myotubes treated with SB203580 or SB202190, however, exhibited a dose dependent increase in caffeine-induced calcium release (Figure 5A–B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 5A-B.

claim: SB203580 and SB202190 impaired caffeine-induced calcium release in control WT C2C12 myotubes.
source: Conversely, these chemicals impaired caffeine-induced calcium release in control WT C2C12 myotubes (Figure 5A–B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 5A-B.

claim: siRNA knockdown of Mapk11 (p38β) promoted increased caffeine-induced calcium release in Ryr1 KO cells versus negative control siRNA.
source: In Ryr1 KO C2C12 cells, siRNA knockdown of Mapk11 (p38β) promoted increased caffeine-induced calcium release in KO cells versus negative control siRNA (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 5C.

claim: Knockdown of Mapk14 (p38α) and Mapk12 (p38γ) increased calcium release in Ryr1 KO myotubes but to a lesser degree than Mapk11 knockdown.
source: Knockdown of Mapk14 (p38α) and Mapk12 (p38γ) also increased calcium release in Ryr1 KO myotubes but to a lesser degree.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a comparison of siRNA effects.

claim: siRNA knockdown of p38 isoforms did not impair Ca2+ release in WT C2C12 cells.
source: Unlike with SB203580 or SB202190 treatment, siRNA knockdown of p38 isoforms did not impair Ca2+ release in WT cells (Figure 5C)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 5C.

claim: Overnight incubation of YS myotubes with 10 μM SB203580 significantly reduced the temperature-dependent increase in resting Ca2+.
source: Overnight incubation of YS myotubes with 10 μM SB203580 significantly reduced the temperature-dependent increase in resting Ca2+ observed in YS myotubes (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 5D.

claim: The YS model contains a point mutation analogous to the Y522S mutation found in patients with malignant hyperthermia and central core pathology.
source: The YS model contains a point mutation analogous to the Y522S mutation found in patients with malignant hyperthermia and central core pathology (Quane et al., 1994).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citation.

claim: The YS mutation enhances the sensitivity of RyR1 to activators.
source: The YS mutation enhances both the sensitivity of RyR1 to activators (e.g. DHPR, caffeine, 4-chloro-m-cresol) and the temperature-dependence of RyR1 Ca2+ leak, alterations that underlie the MH susceptibility and exertional heat stroke phenotypes of these mice (Chelu et al., 2006; Durham et al., 2008; Lanner et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citations.

claim: The YS mutation enhances the temperature-dependence of RyR1 Ca2+ leak.
source: The YS mutation enhances both the sensitivity of RyR1 to activators (e.g. DHPR, caffeine, 4-chloro-m-cresol) and the temperature-dependence of RyR1 Ca2+ leak, alterations that underlie the MH susceptibility and exertional heat stroke phenotypes of these mice (Chelu et al., 2006; Durham et al., 2008; Lanner et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citations.

claim: The initial screen in C. elegans was completed within two weeks.
source: In terms of speed, the initial screen in C. elegans was completed within two weeks, while the large-scale screen in zebrafish was accomplished in one month.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a description of the pipeline's efficiency.

claim: The large-scale screen in zebrafish was accomplished in one month.
source: In terms of speed, the initial screen in C. elegans was completed within two weeks, while the large-scale screen in zebrafish was accomplished in one month.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a description of the pipeline's efficiency.

claim: Combined treatment of N-acetylcysteine (NAC) and the p38 inhibitor SB203580 leads to robust expansion of myogenic satellite cell populations in vitro and in vivo.
source: Interestingly, it was shown recently that combined treatment of N-acetylcysteine (NAC) and the p38 inhibitor SB203580 leads to robust expansion of myogenic satellite cell populations in vitro and in vivo (L'honoré et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by citation.

claim: NAC has been shown to reduce aberrant oxidative stress and improve phenotypes of preclinical RYR1-RM models.
source: This is noteworthy because NAC has been shown to reduce aberrant oxidative stress and improve phenotypes of preclinical RYR1-RM models (zebrafish and patient cells) (Dowling et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by citation.

claim: p38 inhibition in endothelial cells increased calcium entry via SOCE activation through a mechanism of blocking STIM1 phosphorylation.
source: Interestingly, a previous study in endothelial cells showed that p38 inhibition (chemical and siRNA mediated) increased calcium entry via SOCE activation through a mechanism of blocking STIM1 phosphorylation (Sundivakkam et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by citation.

claim: Gain-of-function mutations in egl-19, the C. elegans homolog of DHPR, suppress the effects of nemadipine-A.
source: This would be consistent with the observation that gain-of-function mutations in egl-19, theC. eleganshomolog of DHPR, suppress the effects of nemadipine-A (Kwok et al., 2006)
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by citation.

claim: DHPR has previously been shown to interact with and activated by RyR3.
source: This mechanism could also explain the observed benefit of p38 inhibition in C2C12 myotubes, as DHPR has previously been shown to interact with and activated by RyR3 (Sheridan et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by citation.

claim: The ryr1a; ryr1b double mutants exhibit no movement and have a median survival of 5 days of life.
source: ryr1a; ryr1b double mutants exhibit no movement and have a median survival of 5 days of life (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–B; Chagovetz et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 3—figure supplement 1A-B and citation.

claim: There are currently no human patients with bi-allelic null mutations in RYR1.
source: There are currently no human patients with bi-allelic null mutations, and thus our models do not accurately mirror the human disease.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a limitation of the models used.

claim: Seven RYR1-RM equivalent mutations in unc-68 were modeled by transgenic overexpression in C. elegans and these mutants exhibited hypersensitivity to caffeine and halothane.
source: In addition, seven RYR1-RM equivalent mutations in unc-68 were modeled by transgenic overexpression in C. elegans and these mutants exhibited hypersensitivity to caffeine and the malignant hyperthermia triggering agent halothane (Baines et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by citation.

claim: p38 inhibition modulates non-RyR1 calcium channels in Ryr1 KO C2C12 cells.
source: Our observation of increased caffeine-induced intracellular calcium release in Ryr1 KO C2C12 cells suggesting that p38 inhibition modulates non-RyR1 calcium channels.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that p38 inhibition promotes calcium release in cells lacking RyR1.

claim: The multi-species platform developed in this study is potentially applicable to a broad range of neuromuscular disorders.
source: This unique platform for RYR1-RM therapy development is potentially applicable to a broad range of neuromuscular disorders.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a broader implication of the work.

claim: The pipeline is based on the functional conservation of RyR1 across many species.
source: This pipeline is based on the functional conservation of RyR1 across many species, and takes advantage of specific attributes of C. elegans (ability to rapidly screen thousands of compounds), zebrafish (large-scale testing in a vertebrate model), and mammalian cell lines (translatability to humans).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as the rationale for the multi-species approach.

claim: C. elegans has the ability to rapidly screen thousands of compounds.
source: This pipeline is based on the functional conservation of RyR1 across many species, and takes advantage of specific attributes of C. elegans (ability to rapidly screen thousands of compounds), zebrafish (large-scale testing in a vertebrate model), and mammalian cell lines (translatability to humans).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as an advantage of using C. elegans.

claim: Zebrafish allows large-scale testing in a vertebrate model.
source: This pipeline is based on the functional conservation of RyR1 across many species, and takes advantage of specific attributes of C. elegans (ability to rapidly screen thousands of compounds), zebrafish (large-scale testing in a vertebrate model), and mammalian cell lines (translatability to humans).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as an advantage of using zebrafish.

claim: Mammalian cell lines provide translatability to humans.
source: This pipeline is based on the functional conservation of RyR1 across many species, and takes advantage of specific attributes of C. elegans (ability to rapidly screen thousands of compounds), zebrafish (large-scale testing in a vertebrate model), and mammalian cell lines (translatability to humans).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as an advantage of using mammalian cell lines.

claim: EGFR inhibitors were overrepresented among the hits from the kinase inhibitor library.
source: Additionally, from the 44 hits in the kinase library we found that EGFR, PERK, and PLK1 inhibitors were overrepresented (**p=0.0060, *p=0.0109, *p=0.0326, respectively).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by statistical analysis.

claim: PERK inhibitors were overrepresented among the hits from the kinase inhibitor library.
source: Additionally, from the 44 hits in the kinase library we found that EGFR, PERK, and PLK1 inhibitors were overrepresented (**p=0.0060, *p=0.0109, *p=0.0326, respectively).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by statistical analysis.

claim: PLK1 inhibitors were overrepresented among the hits from the kinase inhibitor library.
source: Additionally, from the 44 hits in the kinase library we found that EGFR, PERK, and PLK1 inhibitors were overrepresented (**p=0.0060, *p=0.0109, *p=0.0326, respectively).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by statistical analysis.

claim: Multiple GSK3 inhibitors (n = 9) strongly suppressed the unc-68 phenotype but were not statistically overrepresented.
source: Multiple GSK3 (n = 9) and PI3K (n = 3) inhibitors also strongly suppressed the phenotype, but these were not statistically overrepresented (p=0.4093 and p=0.1027, respectively).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with statistical analysis.

claim: Multiple PI3K inhibitors (n = 3) strongly suppressed the unc-68 phenotype but were not statistically overrepresented.
source: Multiple GSK3 (n = 9) and PI3K (n = 3) inhibitors also strongly suppressed the phenotype, but these were not statistically overrepresented (p=0.4093 and p=0.1027, respectively).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with statistical analysis.

claim: Riboflavins were overrepresented among the 18 positive hits from the MicroSource library.
source: Among the 18 positive hits from the MicroSource library, several chemical classes were overrepresented (Figure 2—figure supplement 5): riboflavins (***p=0.0002), surfactants (***p=0.0002), benzophenones (**p=0.0018), anthracenes (*p=0.0279), salicylates (*p=0.0416), and tricyclic antihistamines (*p=0.0416).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 2—figure supplement 5 and statistical analysis.

claim: Surfactants were overrepresented among the 18 positive hits from the MicroSource library.
source: Among the 18 positive hits from the MicroSource library, several chemical classes were overrepresented (Figure 2—figure supplement 5): riboflavins (***p=0.0002), surfactants (***p=0.0002), benzophenones (**p=0.0018), anthracenes (*p=0.0279), salicylates (*p=0.0416), and tricyclic antihistamines (*p=0.0416).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 2—figure supplement 5 and statistical analysis.

claim: Benzophenones were overrepresented among the 18 positive hits from the MicroSource library.
source: Among the 18 positive hits from the MicroSource library, several chemical classes were overrepresented (Figure 2—figure supplement 5): riboflavins (***p=0.0002), surfactants (***p=0.0002), benzophenones (**p=0.0018), anthracenes (*p=0.0279), salicylates (*p=0.0416), and tricyclic antihistamines (*p=0.0416).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 2—figure supplement 5 and statistical analysis.

claim: Anthracenes were overrepresented among the 18 positive hits from the MicroSource library.
source: Among the 18 positive hits from the MicroSource library, several chemical classes were overrepresented (Figure 2—figure supplement 5): riboflavins (***p=0.0002), surfactants (***p=0.0002), benzophenones (**p=0.0018), anthracenes (*p=0.0279), salicylates (*p=0.0416), and tricyclic antihistamines (*p=0.0416).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 2—figure supplement 5 and statistical analysis.

claim: Salicylates were overrepresented among the 18 positive hits from the MicroSource library.
source: Among the 18 positive hits from the MicroSource library, several chemical classes were overrepresented (Figure 2—figure supplement 5): riboflavins (***p=0.0002), surfactants (***p=0.0002), benzophenones (**p=0.0018), anthracenes (*p=0.0279), salicylates (*p=0.0416), and tricyclic antihistamines (*p=0.0416).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 2—figure supplement 5 and statistical analysis.

claim: Tricyclic antihistamines were overrepresented among the 18 positive hits from the MicroSource library.
source: Among the 18 positive hits from the MicroSource library, several chemical classes were overrepresented (Figure 2—figure supplement 5): riboflavins (***p=0.0002), surfactants (***p=0.0002), benzophenones (**p=0.0018), anthracenes (*p=0.0279), salicylates (*p=0.0416), and tricyclic antihistamines (*p=0.0416).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 2—figure supplement 5 and statistical analysis.

claim: Two DHPR inhibitors out of nine present in the MicroSource library were identified as suppressors of the growth arrest induced by nemadipine-A.
source: Interestingly, two DHPR inhibitors out of nine present in the library (**p=0.0063) were identified as suppressors of the growth arrest induced by nemadipine-A, itself a DHPR inhibitor.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by statistical analysis.

claim: Riboflavin and riboflavin 5-phosphate sodium both strongly suppressed growth arrest in unc-68 mutants.
source: Of note, riboflavin and riboflavin 5-phosphate sodium both strongly suppressed growth arrest (Figure 2—figure supplement 4A,E) and they appear to be structurally distinct from every other chemical in the US Drug Collection (cluster 11, Figure 2—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 2—figure supplement 4A,E and Figure 2—figure supplement 5.

claim: Thiostrepton strongly suppressed growth arrest in unc-68 mutants.
source: Similarly, thiostrepton suppressed growth arrest strongly (Figure 2—figure supplement 4E), is a structurally unique molecule and overrepresented among the 18 hits (*p=0.0141).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 2—figure supplement 4E and statistical analysis.

claim: Thiostrepton is overrepresented among the 18 hits from the MicroSource library.
source: Similarly, thiostrepton suppressed growth arrest strongly (Figure 2—figure supplement 4E), is a structurally unique molecule and overrepresented among the 18 hits (*p=0.0141).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by statistical analysis.

claim: Significant positive interactions were found for three wactives in the zebrafish optogenetic motility assay.
source: Additionally, we found significant positive interactions for three wactives, a PI3K inhibitor, and the anti-psoriatic drug anthralin (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 4—figure supplement 1A-E.

claim: A significant positive interaction was found for a PI3K inhibitor in the zebrafish optogenetic motility assay.
source: Additionally, we found significant positive interactions for three wactives, a PI3K inhibitor, and the anti-psoriatic drug anthralin (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 4—figure supplement 1A-E.

source: Notably, we did not identify any chemicals that significantly improved ryr1b mutant movement speed relative to untreated mutant controls.

claim: Chemical-genetic interactions were not observed for p38 inhibitors SB203580 and SB202190 in the zebrafish optogenetic motility assay.

evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 4C-D.

claim: Roughly 50-80% knockdown of p38 MAPK targets was achieved using commercially available siRNA compared to non-targeting negative control siRNA.
source: Using commercially available siRNA we achieved roughly 50–80% knockdown of p38 MAPK targets as compared to non-targeting negative control siRNA (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: siRNA knockdown of either the α, β, or γ isoforms of p38 prevents C2C12 myoblast differentiation into myotubes.
source: It is important to note that siRNA knockdown was started after differentiation into myotubes because siRNA knockdown of either the α, β, or γ isoforms of p38 prevents C2C12 myoblast differentiation into myotubes (Wang et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the Methods section and supported by citation.

claim: The concentration range of 25-60 μM is used for C. elegans screens to overcome the poor bioaccumulation of exogenous compounds.
source: The concentration used for the latter two libraries was based on previous C. elegans screens performed in the 25–60 μM range (Kwok et al., 2006; Burns et al., 2010; Otten et al., 2018). This concentration range is used to overcome the poor bioaccumulation of exogenous compounds in C. elegans (Burns et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citations.

claim: 145 of the 278 chemicals were prioritized for re-testing because they demonstrated in duplicate wells the most complete suppression of the phenotype.
source: We prioritized 145 of the 278 chemicals for re-testing because they demonstrated in duplicate wells the most complete (i.e. highest number of L4 and adult) suppression the phenotype.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a description of the prioritization strategy.

claim: 142 of the original 278 chemical wells were statistically different from random escapee wells in post-hoc analysis.
source: We estimated the % arrest based on this assumption, using a formula where the number of L1-L3 larvae = 20 –(true count of L4-adult) and found that 142 of the original 278 chemical wells were statistically different from random escapee wells (Figure 2—figure supplements 2–3).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 2—figure supplements 2-3.

claim: 88% of the chemicals identified as statistically significant in post-hoc analysis were in the prioritization group of 145.
source: Given that 88% of those identified as statistically significant were in our prioritization group of 145, this provided us with confidence that they merited additional examination.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as validation of the prioritization strategy.

claim: The unc-68(r1162) strain TR2171 was selected for screening because its growth rate was comparable to N2 wild type.
source: The unc-68(r1162) strain TR2171 was selected for screening because its growth rate was comparable to N2 wild type whereas strain TR2170 grew noticeably slower than N2.
evidence: This is stated in the Methods section as a rationale for strain selection.

claim: Variability in the ryr1b single mutant motor phenotype precluded large-scale screening in zebrafish.
